questions.explanation: Bolívar led independence movements against Spanish colonial rule across northern South America.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi's 1930 Salt March was an act of civil disobedience against a monopoly and tax imposed by which colonial power?
questions.explanation: The Salt March protested the British salt monopoly and tax in colonial India.

questions.question: Nelson Mandela became the first democratically elected president of South Africa in which year?
questions.explanation: Mandela was elected president in South Africa's first fully democratic elections in 1994.

questions.question: Catherine the Great was an influential 18th-century empress of which country?
questions.explanation: Catherine the Great reigned as Empress of Russia from 1762 to 1796.

questions.question: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk is regarded as the founder of the modern republic of which country?
questions.explanation: Atatürk founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923 and served as its first president.

questions.question: Which 18th-century economist introduced the metaphor of the 'invisible hand' in his work The Wealth of Nations?
questions.explanation: Adam Smith's 1776 The Wealth of Nations popularized the 'invisible hand' of the market.

questions.question: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels co-authored which 1848 political pamphlet?
questions.explanation: Marx and Engels wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1848; Das Kapital was authored by Marx alone later.

questions.question: The economic theory advocating increased government spending to stimulate demand during recessions is most associated with which economist?
questions.explanation: Keynesian economics, from John Maynard Keynes, advocates active fiscal policy to manage demand.

questions.question: The 1944 Bretton Woods Conference led to the creation of the International Monetary Fund and which other institution?
questions.explanation: Bretton Woods established both the IMF and the World Bank (originally the IBRD).

questions.question: The economic theory of comparative advantage in international trade was formulated by which economist?
questions.explanation: David Ricardo articulated the theory of comparative advantage in the early 19th century.

questions.question: The Marshall Plan was a U.S. program that provided economic aid primarily to rebuild which region after World War II?
questions.explanation: The Marshall Plan (1948) funneled U.S. aid into the reconstruction of Western Europe.

questions.question: In Norse mythology, what is the name of the prophesied cataclysm in which many gods die in a final battle?
questions.explanation: Ragnarök is the foretold series of events, including a great battle, that brings the death of many Norse gods.

questions.question: In Hinduism, the Trimurti consists of Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, and which deity as the destroyer?
questions.explanation: Shiva completes the Trimurti as the destroyer or transformer alongside Brahma and Vishnu.

questions.question: In ancient Egyptian mythology, which god was the ruler of the underworld and judge of the dead?
questions.explanation: Osiris ruled the Egyptian underworld and presided over the judgment of the dead.

questions.question: The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path are central teachings of which religion?
questions.explanation: The Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path are foundational teachings of Buddhism.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the Five Pillars of Islam?
questions.explanation: Zakat, obligatory almsgiving, is one of the Five Pillars of Islam alongside Shahada, Salat, Sawm, and Hajj; the Hajj pilgrimage is to Mecca, not Jerusalem.

questions.question: The Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the earliest surviving works of literature, originated in which ancient region?
questions.explanation: The Epic of Gilgamesh comes from ancient Mesopotamia, with roots in Sumerian and later Babylonian texts.

questions.question: The Greek goddess Athena, associated with wisdom and warfare, corresponds to which Roman goddess?
questions.explanation: Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom, equivalent to the Greek Athena.

questions.question: Winston Churchill popularized which phrase in a 1946 speech to describe the division of Europe during the Cold War?
questions.explanation: In his 1946 Fulton, Missouri speech, Churchill declared that an 'Iron Curtain' had descended across Europe.

questions.question: The Congress of Vienna (1814–1815) was convened primarily to reorganize Europe after the downfall of whom?
questions.explanation: The Congress of Vienna redrew Europe's map following the defeat of Napoleon.

questions.question: The Black Death that devastated 14th-century Europe is generally attributed to which disease?
questions.explanation: The Black Death is widely believed to have been an outbreak of bubonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis.

questions.question: Johannes Gutenberg is credited with introducing which technology to Europe around 1440?
questions.explanation: Gutenberg developed the movable-type printing press in Europe around 1440.

questions.question: The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804) created the first nation led by former slaves, winning independence from which country?
questions.explanation: Haiti won independence from France in 1804 after a slave-led revolution.

questions.question: Under which sultan, known in the West as 'the Magnificent,' did the Ottoman Empire reach a 16th-century peak of power?
questions.explanation: Suleiman I ('the Magnificent') presided over the Ottoman Empire's golden age in the 16th century.

questions.question: The United States Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Continental Congress in which year?
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on 4 July 1776.

questions.question: The Allied invasion of Normandy on 6 June 1944 is commonly known by what name?
questions.explanation: The 6 June 1944 Normandy landings are known as D-Day; Operation Barbarossa was Germany's 1941 invasion of the USSR.

questions.question: The Long March of 1934–1935 was a strategic retreat undertaken by the Red Army of which party?
questions.explanation: The Long March was carried out by the Chinese Communist Party's Red Army to escape Kuomintang forces.

questions.question: In Norse cosmology, what is Yggdrasil?
options: An immense world tree connecting the nine realms
The ship built from the dead
questions.explanation: Yggdrasil is the vast world tree at the center of the Norse cosmos, linking the nine realms.

questions.question: The Bhagavad Gita, a key Hindu scripture, forms part of which larger epic?
questions.explanation: The Bhagavad Gita is a dialogue embedded within the epic Mahabharata.

questions.question: The political doctrine of separating government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches was notably developed by which Enlightenment thinker?
questions.explanation: Montesquieu developed the theory of the separation of powers in his 1748 work The Spirit of the Laws.

questions.question: The English Civil War of the 1640s culminated in the 1649 execution of which king?
questions.explanation: King Charles I was tried and executed in 1649 after Parliament's victory in the English Civil War.

questions.question: The League of Nations, founded after World War I, was notably never joined by which major power?
questions.explanation: Despite President Wilson's advocacy, the U.S. Senate rejected membership, so the United States never joined the League.

questions.question: The 1992 Maastricht Treaty formally established which organization?
questions.explanation: The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Union; the EEC dated from the 1957 Treaty of Rome.

questions.question: The Aztec Empire was conquered in the early 16th century by a Spanish expedition led by whom?
questions.explanation: Hernán Cortés led the conquest of the Aztec Empire; Pizarro conquered the Inca.

questions.question: The Inca Empire, conquered by Francisco Pizarro in the 1530s, had its capital at which city?
questions.explanation: Cusco was the capital of the Inca Empire; Tenochtitlan was the Aztec capital.

questions.question: The 1773 Boston Tea Party was a colonial protest most directly against which piece of British legislation?
questions.explanation: The Boston Tea Party protested the Tea Act, which granted the British East India Company a tea monopoly.

questions.question: In Greek mythology, the Titan Prometheus is best known for which act?
options: Stealing fire from the gods and giving it to humanity
Opening a jar that released evils into the world
Slaying the Minotaur in the labyrinth
Holding up the sky on his shoulders
questions.explanation: Prometheus stole fire from the gods for humanity; Pandora opened the jar, Theseus slew the Minotaur, and Atlas held up the sky.

questions.question: In Egyptian mythology, the jackal-headed god associated with mummification and embalming was:
questions.explanation: Anubis, depicted with a jackal's head, was the Egyptian god of mummification and the dead.

questions.question: A political system in which power is concentrated in the hands of a small, privileged group is known as:
questions.explanation: An oligarchy is rule by a small group; a theocracy is rule by religious authority and an autocracy is rule by one person.

questions.question: In economics, a situation combining stagnant growth, high unemployment, and rising prices is called:
questions.explanation: Stagflation describes the simultaneous occurrence of economic stagnation (with high unemployment) and inflation.

questions.question: Under the classical gold standard, a nation's currency value is directly tied to:
questions.explanation: The gold standard fixes a currency's value to a specific amount of gold.

questions.question: The Berlin Wall, which divided East and West Berlin, fell in which year?
questions.explanation: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, presaging German reunification in 1990.

questions.question: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 (the Sepoy Mutiny) was directed against the rule of which entity?
questions.explanation: The 1857 rebellion was against the British East India Company, whose rule was afterward transferred to the British Crown.

questions.question: Newton's third law of motion is best summarized by which statement?
options: Objects at rest stay at rest unless acted on by a force
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
Every mass attracts every other mass
questions.explanation: Newton's third law states that for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons, the force needed to accelerate one kilogram at one metre per second squared.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of power?
questions.explanation: Power, the rate of energy transfer, is measured in watts (one joule per second).

questions.question: The speed of a wave equals its frequency multiplied by its what?
questions.explanation: The wave equation v = f x lambda means speed equals frequency times wavelength.

questions.question: Sound travels through air as which type of wave?
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal wave in which air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel.

questions.question: Which principle states that the upward buoyant force on a submerged object equals the weight of fluid it displaces?
questions.explanation: Archimedes' principle explains buoyancy: the upthrust equals the weight of the displaced fluid.

questions.question: Approximately what is the acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: Objects in free fall near Earth's surface accelerate at about 9.8 metres per second squared.

questions.question: The Doppler effect describes the apparent change in a wave's what, due to relative motion between source and observer?
questions.explanation: The Doppler effect is the shift in observed frequency (such as pitch) caused by relative motion of source and observer.

questions.question: According to Ohm's law, voltage equals current multiplied by what?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law is V = I x R, so voltage equals current times resistance.

questions.question: The first law of thermodynamics is essentially a statement of the conservation of what?
questions.explanation: The first law of thermodynamics is the principle of conservation of energy applied to heat and work.

questions.question: According to the second law of thermodynamics, the total entropy of an isolated system tends to do what?
questions.explanation: The second law states that the entropy (disorder) of an isolated system tends to increase over time.

questions.question: Which physical quantity is defined as mass multiplied by velocity?
questions.explanation: Linear momentum is the product of an object's mass and its velocity (p = m x v).

questions.question: Hooke's law states that, within the elastic limit, the extension of a spring is directly proportional to what?
questions.explanation: Hooke's law says extension is proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit (F = kx).

questions.question: Heat can be transferred across the vacuum of space only by which process?
questions.explanation: Radiation transfers heat as electromagnetic waves and needs no medium, so it works through a vacuum.

questions.question: The temperature at which molecular motion theoretically stops, equal to 0 kelvin, is called what?
questions.explanation: Absolute zero (0 K, about -273.15 C) is the lowest possible temperature, where particle motion is minimal.

questions.question: What is the chemical formula for water?
questions.explanation: Water consists of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, giving the formula H2O.

questions.question: The compound with the formula NaCl is commonly known as what?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is ordinary table salt.

questions.question: Which gas turns limewater milky, a classic test for its presence?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form insoluble calcium carbonate, turning it milky.

questions.question: A solution with a pH of exactly 7 is described as what?
questions.explanation: A pH of 7 is neutral, neither acidic nor basic, like pure water.

questions.question: Which industrial process combines nitrogen and hydrogen to produce ammonia?
questions.explanation: The Haber process synthesises ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen under high pressure and temperature with an iron catalyst.

questions.question: The Contact process is used to manufacture which acid industrially?
questions.explanation: The Contact process produces sulfuric acid by oxidising sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide.

questions.question: A chemical reaction that releases heat to its surroundings is described as what?
questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions release energy, usually as heat, to the surroundings.

questions.question: Methane, the simplest hydrocarbon, has which chemical formula?
questions.explanation: Methane is the simplest alkane, one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms (CH4).

questions.question: Hydrocarbons that contain only single carbon-carbon bonds are called what?
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing only single C-C bonds.

questions.question: When an acid reacts with a base, the products are a salt and what?
questions.explanation: Neutralisation of an acid by a base produces a salt and water.

questions.question: During electrolysis, positively charged ions (cations) move toward which electrode?
questions.explanation: Cations are attracted to the negatively charged cathode during electrolysis.

questions.question: Baking soda is the common name for which compound?
questions.explanation: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate (sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO3).

questions.question: The process by which a solid changes directly into a gas without becoming liquid is called what?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is the direct solid-to-gas transition, as seen with dry ice.

questions.question: The rusting of iron is an example of which chemical process?
questions.explanation: Rusting is the oxidation of iron in the presence of oxygen and water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide.

questions.question: Which indicator is colourless in acid but turns pink in an alkaline (basic) solution?
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution and pink in basic solution.

questions.question: Which organelle is often called the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria generate most of the cell's ATP through respiration, earning the nickname 'powerhouse of the cell'.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are found in a typical human body cell?
questions.explanation: Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs.

questions.question: In DNA, the base adenine always pairs with which other base?
questions.explanation: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine (and guanine with cytosine) through hydrogen bonds.

questions.question: Who is regarded as the 'father of genetics' for his work on inheritance in pea plants?
questions.explanation: Gregor Mendel's pea-plant experiments established the basic laws of inheritance.

questions.question: Which gas is released by plants as a by-product of photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis splits water and releases oxygen as a by-product.

questions.question: Enzymes are biological molecules that act as what?
questions.explanation: Enzymes are protein catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions without being consumed.

questions.question: Which type of cell division produces gametes with half the normal chromosome number?
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce haploid gametes.

questions.question: Which of these is the broadest (most inclusive) rank in biological classification?
questions.explanation: In the hierarchy Kingdom > Phylum > Class > Order, kingdom is the broadest of these ranks.

questions.question: An organism that makes its own food, such as a green plant, is called a what?
questions.explanation: Producers (autotrophs) synthesise their own food, typically via photosynthesis.

questions.question: What is the basic structural and functional unit of all living things?
questions.explanation: The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all life processes.

questions.question: The net movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane is called what?
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the net movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration.

questions.question: Which green pigment allows plants to absorb light for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that captures light energy for photosynthesis.

questions.question: A relationship in which both organisms benefit is called what?
questions.explanation: In mutualism, both partner organisms gain a benefit from the relationship.

questions.question: Bacteria are classified as which type of cell?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes: single-celled organisms without a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.question: The growth of a plant shoot toward a light source is called what?
questions.explanation: Phototropism is directional growth in response to light; shoots grow toward it.

questions.question: How many bones are there in the adult human skeleton?
questions.explanation: The mature human skeleton normally contains 206 bones.

questions.question: Which is the longest and largest bone in the human body?
questions.explanation: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone in the body.

questions.question: Which protein in red blood cells carries oxygen around the body?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and transports it through the bloodstream.

questions.question: Which is the largest artery in the human body?
questions.explanation: The aorta is the largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the heart to the body.

questions.question: Which gland is often called the 'master gland' because it controls other endocrine glands?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland regulates many other endocrine glands, earning the name 'master gland'.

questions.question: Which organ filters waste from the blood to produce urine?
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter blood and excrete waste products as urine.

questions.question: How many teeth are there in a full set of adult (permanent) human teeth?
questions.explanation: A complete adult set has 32 permanent teeth, including the four wisdom teeth.

questions.question: The specialised muscle tissue that makes up the heart is called what?
questions.explanation: The heart is made of cardiac muscle, a specialised involuntary striated muscle.

questions.question: Which part of the eye contains the light-sensitive rods and cones?
questions.explanation: The retina at the back of the eye holds the photoreceptor rods and cones.

questions.question: The windpipe, which carries air to the lungs, is properly called what?
questions.explanation: The trachea (windpipe) conducts air between the larynx and the bronchi.

questions.question: Which hormone, released by the adrenal glands, prepares the body for 'fight or flight'?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) from the adrenal glands triggers the fight-or-flight response.

questions.question: How many pairs of ribs does a typical human have?
questions.explanation: Humans normally have 12 pairs of ribs, for a total of 24 ribs.

questions.question: In which organ does most absorption of digested nutrients occur?
questions.explanation: The small intestine, with its villi, absorbs most nutrients from digested food.

questions.question: What is the name of the pale, liquid component of blood in which cells are suspended?
questions.explanation: Plasma is the fluid portion of blood that carries cells, nutrients, and wastes.

questions.question: Which is the longest nerve in the human body?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve, running from the lower back down each leg, is the longest and widest nerve in the body.

questions.question: Which is the closest planet to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Mercury is the innermost planet, orbiting closest to the Sun.

questions.question: Which planet is commonly known as the 'Red Planet'?
questions.explanation: Mars appears red because of iron oxide (rust) on its surface.

questions.question: What is the name of Earth's only natural satellite?
questions.explanation: Earth has a single natural satellite, simply called the Moon.

questions.question: The Milky Way is classified as which type of galaxy?
questions.explanation: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with arms winding out from a central bulge.

questions.question: Who was the first human to walk on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Neil Armstrong was the first person to step onto the Moon, in July 1969.

questions.question: Which is the nearest star to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away, is the closest star to our Sun.

questions.question: The Great Red Spot, a giant persistent storm, is found on which planet?
questions.explanation: The Great Red Spot is a centuries-old storm in Jupiter's atmosphere.

questions.question: According to current cosmology, approximately how old is the universe?
questions.explanation: Measurements place the age of the universe at about 13.8 billion years since the Big Bang.

questions.question: The Sun is classified as which type of star?
questions.explanation: The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star, commonly called a yellow dwarf.

questions.question: Which mission first landed humans on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Apollo 11 carried the first astronauts to land on the Moon in 1969.

questions.question: Which is the brightest star in Earth's night sky?
questions.explanation: Sirius, in the constellation Canis Major, is the brightest star seen from Earth.

questions.question: The explosive death of a massive star is known as a what?
questions.explanation: A supernova is the powerful explosion marking the death of a massive star.

questions.question: About how long does light from the Sun take to reach Earth?
questions.explanation: Sunlight travels the roughly 150 million km to Earth in about 8 minutes.

questions.question: Which star is commonly known as the North Star?
questions.explanation: Polaris sits nearly above Earth's north pole, appearing almost fixed as the North Star.

questions.question: What is the extremely dense collapsed stellar core, composed mainly of neutrons, called?
questions.explanation: A neutron star is the ultra-dense remnant of a massive star's core after a supernova.

questions.question: Who is credited with inventing the first practical telephone?
questions.explanation: Alexander Graham Bell received the first patent for a practical telephone in 1876.

questions.question: Who developed the first commercially practical incandescent light bulb?
questions.explanation: Thomas Edison developed a long-lasting, commercially viable incandescent light bulb.

questions.question: Who discovered X-rays in 1895?
questions.explanation: Wilhelm Rontgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.question: Who built and flew the first powered, controlled aeroplane in 1903?
questions.explanation: Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained powered flight in 1903.

questions.question: Who formulated the law of universal gravitation?
questions.explanation: Isaac Newton formulated the law of universal gravitation in the 17th century.

questions.question: Who discovered radioactivity in 1896?
questions.explanation: Henri Becquerel discovered natural radioactivity while studying uranium salts in 1896.

questions.question: Who invented the World Wide Web?
questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN.

questions.question: Whose improvements to the steam engine helped drive the Industrial Revolution?
questions.explanation: James Watt's greatly improved steam engine became a key power source of the Industrial Revolution.

questions.question: Who invented the first electric battery, the voltaic pile?
questions.explanation: Alessandro Volta invented the voltaic pile, the first true electric battery, around 1800.

questions.question: Who used a telescope to discover the four largest moons of Jupiter?
questions.explanation: Galileo Galilei discovered Jupiter's four largest moons in 1610 with his telescope.

questions.question: Who invented dynamite and later established the Nobel Prizes?
questions.explanation: Alfred Nobel invented dynamite and left his fortune to fund the Nobel Prizes.

questions.question: Who won the Nobel Prize for pioneering long-distance wireless (radio) telegraphy?
questions.explanation: Guglielmo Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize for developing practical wireless telegraphy.

questions.question: Who led the team that discovered insulin as a treatment for diabetes?
questions.explanation: Frederick Banting, with Charles Best, isolated insulin in 1921-22 to treat diabetes.

questions.question: Who introduced the idea that energy is emitted in discrete packets, founding quantum theory?
questions.explanation: Max Planck proposed that energy comes in quanta in 1900, launching quantum theory.

questions.question: Who developed the first successful injectable polio vaccine in the 1950s?
questions.explanation: Jonas Salk developed the first effective inactivated (injectable) polio vaccine in 1955.

questions.question: Which component is often described as the 'brain' of a computer?
questions.explanation: The CPU (central processing unit) executes instructions and is the computer's main processor.

questions.question: How many bits are there in one byte?
questions.explanation: One byte is made up of 8 bits.

questions.question: The binary number system uses which two digits?
questions.explanation: Binary is a base-2 system using only the digits 0 and 1.

questions.question: Who designed the Analytical Engine and is often called the 'father of the computer'?
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage conceived the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose mechanical computer design.

questions.question: Who is widely regarded as the world's first computer programmer?
questions.explanation: Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for Babbage's Analytical Engine, making her the first programmer.

questions.question: The Turing test is a way of assessing a machine's capacity for what?
questions.explanation: The Turing test evaluates whether a machine can exhibit intelligent behaviour indistinguishable from a human.

questions.question: What is HTML primarily used for?
questions.explanation: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) structures the content of web pages.

questions.question: Which type of computer memory is volatile, losing its contents when power is switched off?
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile memory that loses stored data when the computer loses power.

questions.question: Who created the Linux operating system kernel?
questions.explanation: Linus Torvalds released the first Linux kernel in 1991.

questions.question: Which logic gate outputs 'true' only when both of its inputs are 'true'?
questions.explanation: An AND gate outputs true only when all of its inputs are true.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation 'HTTP' stand for?
questions.explanation: HTTP stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol, the basis of data communication on the web.

questions.question: Moore's law famously predicts the growth over time of which quantity?
options: The number of transistors on a chip
questions.explanation: Moore's law observes that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit roughly doubles about every two years.

questions.question: Which is often cited as the first general-purpose electronic digital computer?
questions.explanation: ENIAC, completed in 1945, is widely regarded as the first general-purpose electronic digital computer.

questions.question: Which pioneering computer scientist is associated with popularising the term 'bug' after a moth was found in a machine?
questions.explanation: Grace Hopper's team logged a real moth causing a fault, popularising 'bug' for a computer error.

questions.question: 1024 megabytes is approximately equal to one what?
questions.explanation: 1024 megabytes make up one gigabyte in binary-based measurement.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
questions.explanation: Sodium's symbol is Na, from its Latin name natrium.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?
questions.explanation: Potassium's symbol is K, from its Latin name kalium.

questions.question: Which element is the most abundant in the universe?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is by far the most abundant element in the universe.

questions.question: Which element is the most abundant in the Earth's crust by mass?
questions.explanation: Oxygen makes up roughly 46% of the Earth's crust by mass, more than any other element.

questions.question: Elements in Group 18 of the periodic table are collectively known as the what?
questions.explanation: Group 18 elements, such as helium and neon, are the noble gases, largely unreactive.

questions.question: The chemical symbol 'Pb' refers to which element?
questions.explanation: Pb is the symbol for lead, from its Latin name plumbum.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
questions.explanation: Iron's symbol is Fe, from its Latin name ferrum.

questions.question: Excluding hydrogen, the elements in Group 1 of the periodic table are known as the what?
questions.explanation: Group 1 elements such as lithium, sodium and potassium are the highly reactive alkali metals.

questions.question: Which element is a key component of hemoglobin, letting blood carry oxygen?
questions.explanation: Iron sits at the centre of the heme group in hemoglobin and binds oxygen.

questions.question: Which metal has the highest melting point of all metals?
questions.explanation: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3422 C.

questions.question: Which is the densest naturally occurring element?
questions.explanation: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, slightly denser than iridium.

questions.question: Which metal atom sits at the centre of a chlorophyll molecule?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll contains a central magnesium ion within its porphyrin ring.

questions.question: The chemical symbol 'Ag' represents which element?
questions.explanation: Ag is the symbol for silver, from its Latin name argentum.

questions.question: The halogens occupy which group of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: The halogens, such as fluorine and chlorine, make up Group 17.

questions.question: Which non-metal element is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Bromine is one of only two elements liquid at room temperature and the only liquid non-metal.

questions.question: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.explanation: George Washington served as the first U.S. President from 1789 to 1797.

questions.question: The ancient pyramids at Giza in Egypt were built primarily to serve as what?
questions.explanation: The Giza pyramids were monumental tombs constructed to house and honor deceased pharaohs.

questions.question: Who became the first emperor to unify China in 221 BC?
questions.explanation: Qin Shi Huang unified the warring states and founded the Qin dynasty, becoming China's first emperor.

questions.question: The Battle of Hastings in 1066 led to the Norman conquest of which country?
questions.explanation: William the Conqueror's victory at Hastings in 1066 secured Norman control of England.

questions.question: The Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588 during the reign of which English monarch?
questions.explanation: The Armada's defeat came during the reign of Elizabeth I, marking a high point of Tudor England.

questions.question: Which explorer, sailing on behalf of Spain, reached the Americas in 1492?
questions.explanation: Christopher Columbus, funded by the Spanish crown, made landfall in the Americas in 1492.

questions.question: The Renaissance, a cultural rebirth beginning in the 14th century, originated in which country?
questions.explanation: The Renaissance began in the city-states of Italy, especially Florence, before spreading across Europe.

questions.question: The French king Louis XIV was widely known by which nickname?
questions.explanation: Louis XIV was called the Sun King (le Roi Soleil), symbolizing his absolute, radiant authority.

questions.question: The Edict of Milan (313 AD), granting tolerance to Christians in the Roman Empire, is associated with which emperor?
questions.explanation: Constantine (with Licinius) issued the Edict of Milan, legalizing Christianity across the empire.

questions.question: The Treaty of Verdun (843 AD) divided the Carolingian Empire among the sons of which ruler?
questions.explanation: The treaty split the empire among the three sons of Louis the Pious, Charlemagne's heir.

questions.question: In which year did the American Civil War end?
questions.explanation: The American Civil War ended in 1865 with the surrender of the Confederacy.

questions.question: The Taiping Rebellion, one of the deadliest civil wars in history, took place in which country during the 19th century?
questions.explanation: The Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864) devastated Qing-dynasty China, killing tens of millions.

questions.question: The Peace of Augsburg (1555) established the principle that a ruler could determine his territory's religion, summarized by which Latin phrase?
questions.explanation: 'Cuius regio, eius religio' means 'whose realm, his religion,' letting princes set their land's faith.

questions.question: The partition creating the independent nations of India and Pakistan occurred in which year?
questions.explanation: British India was partitioned into India and Pakistan in 1947.

questions.question: Which queen was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony?
questions.explanation: Cleopatra VII was Egypt's final Ptolemaic ruler, famed for her alliances with Caesar and Antony.

questions.question: Which artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.explanation: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling frescoes between 1508 and 1512.

questions.question: The swirling night sky painting 'The Starry Night' was created by which artist?
questions.explanation: Vincent van Gogh painted 'The Starry Night' in 1889 while at an asylum in Saint-Remy.

questions.question: The art movement pioneered by Claude Monet, emphasizing light and loose brushwork, is called?
questions.explanation: Impressionism, led by Monet, captured fleeting light and atmosphere with visible brushstrokes.

questions.question: Which Spanish artist co-founded the Cubist movement alongside Georges Braque?
questions.explanation: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque jointly developed Cubism in the early 20th century.

questions.question: The famous bronze sculpture 'The Thinker' was created by which artist?
questions.explanation: Auguste Rodin created 'The Thinker,' originally part of his larger work 'The Gates of Hell.'

questions.question: The Surrealist painting 'The Persistence of Memory,' featuring melting clocks, was created by?
questions.explanation: Salvador Dali painted the melting-clock image 'The Persistence of Memory' in 1931.

questions.question: The technique of painting with pigments onto freshly laid wet plaster is known as?
questions.explanation: In fresco, pigment is applied to wet plaster so the color becomes part of the wall as it dries.

questions.question: Which Dutch master painted 'The Night Watch'?
questions.explanation: Rembrandt painted the large group portrait 'The Night Watch' in 1642.

questions.question: Which composer wrote his Ninth Symphony, including the 'Ode to Joy,' after becoming almost completely deaf?
questions.explanation: Beethoven composed his Ninth Symphony while profoundly deaf, premiering it in 1824.

questions.question: The set of violin concertos known as 'The Four Seasons' was composed by?
questions.explanation: Antonio Vivaldi composed 'The Four Seasons,' four concertos each depicting a season.

questions.question: Which Austrian composer wrote the operas 'The Magic Flute' and 'Don Giovanni'?
questions.explanation: Mozart composed both 'The Magic Flute' and 'Don Giovanni' among his celebrated operas.

questions.question: In music, the term describing the speed or pace at which a piece is played is?
questions.explanation: Tempo refers to the speed of a piece, often marked with terms like allegro or adagio.

questions.question: How many strings does a standard violin have?
questions.explanation: A standard violin has four strings, tuned G, D, A, and E.

questions.question: Which Baroque composer wrote the six 'Brandenburg Concertos'?
questions.explanation: J.S. Bach composed the six Brandenburg Concertos, dedicating them in 1721.

questions.question: Which clef is commonly used for higher-pitched instruments and the right hand of the piano?
questions.explanation: The treble (G) clef notates higher pitches and is used for the piano's right hand.

questions.question: Who is traditionally credited as the author of the ancient Greek epics 'The Iliad' and 'The Odyssey'?
questions.explanation: Homer is traditionally credited with composing both 'The Iliad' and 'The Odyssey.'

questions.question: Which author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
questions.explanation: Arthur Conan Doyle created Sherlock Holmes, first appearing in 'A Study in Scarlet' (1887).

questions.question: The epic novel 'War and Peace' was written by which Russian author?
questions.explanation: Leo Tolstoy wrote 'War and Peace,' published in the 1860s.

questions.question: Who wrote 'The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'?
questions.explanation: Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens) wrote 'The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn' in 1884.

questions.question: The novel 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' was written by which Colombian author?
questions.explanation: Gabriel Garcia Marquez wrote this landmark of magical realism, published in 1967.

questions.question: Which English playwright wrote the tragedies 'Hamlet' and 'Macbeth'?
questions.explanation: William Shakespeare wrote both 'Hamlet' and 'Macbeth' among his tragedies.

questions.question: The 14th-century epic poem 'The Divine Comedy' was written by which Italian poet?
questions.explanation: Dante Alighieri wrote 'The Divine Comedy,' describing a journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise.

questions.question: Which Russian author wrote 'Crime and Punishment'?
questions.explanation: Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote 'Crime and Punishment,' published in 1866.

questions.question: 'Don Quixote,' often called the first modern novel, was written by?
questions.explanation: Miguel de Cervantes wrote 'Don Quixote,' published in two parts in 1605 and 1615.

questions.question: Who wrote the dystopian novel 'Brave New World'?
questions.explanation: Aldous Huxley wrote 'Brave New World' in 1932, depicting a rigidly engineered future society.

questions.question: The ancient Indian epic 'Ramayana' is traditionally attributed to which sage?
questions.explanation: The sage Valmiki is traditionally credited as the author of the Sanskrit 'Ramayana.'

questions.question: Which American writer authored the poem 'The Raven'?
questions.explanation: Edgar Allan Poe published 'The Raven,' with its refrain 'Nevermore,' in 1845.

questions.question: The influential novel 'Things Fall Apart' was written by which Nigerian author?
questions.explanation: Chinua Achebe wrote 'Things Fall Apart' (1958), a cornerstone of modern African literature.

questions.question: The 'Harry Potter' fantasy series was written by?
questions.explanation: J.K. Rowling wrote the seven-book 'Harry Potter' series, beginning in 1997.

questions.question: Who wrote 'The Canterbury Tales' in Middle English?
questions.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote 'The Canterbury Tales' in the late 14th century.

questions.question: How often are the modern Summer Olympic Games normally held?
questions.explanation: The Summer Olympic Games are held every four years, an interval known as an Olympiad.

questions.question: In which sport would a player perform a 'slam dunk'?
questions.explanation: A slam dunk, forcing the ball down through the hoop, is a basketball move.

questions.question: How many players make up a cricket team on the field?
questions.explanation: A cricket team fields eleven players.

questions.question: In tennis scoring, which term denotes a score of zero?
questions.explanation: In tennis, 'love' means a score of zero.

questions.question: The Tour de France is a premier competition in which sport?
questions.explanation: The Tour de France is the world's most famous multi-stage road cycling race.

questions.question: In American football, how many points is a touchdown worth (before the extra point)?
questions.explanation: A touchdown is worth six points, with a conversion attempt awarded afterward.

questions.question: In chess, which piece moves only diagonally?
questions.explanation: The bishop moves any number of squares diagonally, staying on one color.

questions.question: In football (soccer), a 'hat-trick' is achieved when one player scores how many goals in a match?
questions.explanation: A hat-trick is scoring three goals in a single match.

questions.question: The Wimbledon tennis championships are traditionally played on which court surface?
questions.explanation: Wimbledon is the only Grand Slam still played on grass courts.

questions.question: In golf, what is the term for completing a hole in one stroke under par?
questions.explanation: A birdie is one stroke under par; an eagle is two under.

questions.question: How many squares are there on a standard chessboard?
questions.explanation: A chessboard has an 8x8 grid, totaling 64 squares.

questions.question: In which country did the martial art of judo originate?
questions.explanation: Judo was founded in Japan by Jigoro Kano in 1882.

questions.question: In baseball, how many strikes result in a strikeout?
questions.explanation: Three strikes constitute a strikeout, putting the batter out.

questions.question: In which sport is the Ryder Cup contested?
questions.explanation: The Ryder Cup is a team golf competition between Europe and the United States.

questions.question: In snooker, what is the maximum possible break in a single frame without opponent fouls?
questions.explanation: A maximum break of 147 comes from potting all reds with blacks, then all colors.

questions.question: The Amazon River flows through which continent?
questions.explanation: The Amazon, the world's largest river by discharge, flows through South America.

questions.question: Which continent is the coldest and covered almost entirely by ice?
questions.explanation: Antarctica is the coldest continent, blanketed by a permanent ice sheet.

questions.question: Which is the smallest of the seven continents by land area?
questions.explanation: Australia is the smallest continent by land area.

questions.question: The Equator passes directly through which of these countries?
questions.explanation: The Equator runs through Ecuador, which is named for it (equator in Spanish).

questions.question: Mount Everest is part of which mountain range?
questions.explanation: Mount Everest lies in the Himalayas on the Nepal-China border.

questions.question: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the northeastern coast of which country?
questions.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along the coast of Queensland, Australia.

questions.question: The Prime Meridian (0 degrees longitude) is defined as passing through which area of London?
questions.explanation: The Prime Meridian passes through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London.

questions.question: The Nile River empties into which sea?
questions.explanation: The Nile flows northward and drains into the Mediterranean Sea via its delta in Egypt.

questions.question: The line of latitude located at approximately 23.5 degrees North is called the?
questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer lies at about 23.5 degrees North, the sun's northernmost overhead point.

questions.question: Norway's coastline is famous for deep, narrow sea inlets carved by glaciers, known as?
questions.explanation: Fjords are steep glacially carved inlets, a hallmark of Norway's coastline.

questions.question: The Iberian Peninsula is occupied mainly by which two countries?
questions.explanation: Spain and Portugal make up most of the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe.

questions.question: The Dead Sea, the lowest exposed land point on Earth, borders Jordan and which other country?
questions.explanation: The Dead Sea lies between Jordan and Israel (along the West Bank).

questions.question: The historic trading city of Timbuktu is located in which African country?
questions.explanation: Timbuktu, a famed center of trade and learning, lies in modern Mali.

questions.question: The Strait of Gibraltar connects the Mediterranean Sea to which ocean?
questions.explanation: The Strait of Gibraltar links the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.question: The Gobi Desert spans southern Mongolia and which other country?
questions.explanation: The Gobi Desert covers parts of southern Mongolia and northern China.

questions.question: The Eiffel Tower is a landmark of which city?
questions.explanation: The Eiffel Tower, built in 1889, is an iconic landmark of Paris.

questions.question: The Statue of Liberty in New York was a gift to the United States from which country?
questions.explanation: France gifted the Statue of Liberty to the United States, dedicated in 1886.

questions.question: The Colosseum, an ancient amphitheatre, is located in which city?
questions.explanation: The Colosseum, completed around AD 80, stands in Rome.

questions.question: The Taj Mahal, a white marble mausoleum, is located in which country?
questions.explanation: The Taj Mahal was built in Agra, India, by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

questions.question: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built as a tomb for which pharaoh?
questions.explanation: The Great Pyramid was built for Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops) of the Fourth Dynasty.

questions.question: Which word is a synonym for "happy"?
questions.explanation: "Joyful" means feeling or showing great happiness, making it a synonym for "happy."

questions.question: What is the antonym of "ancient"?
questions.explanation: "Modern" means relating to the present time, the opposite of "ancient," which means very old. "Old," "historic," and "aged" are near-synonyms of ancient.

questions.question: What part of speech is the word "quickly"?
questions.explanation: "Quickly" modifies a verb by describing how an action is performed, so it is an adverb.

questions.question: Which is the correct spelling?
questions.explanation: "Receive" follows the guideline "i before e except after c"; because the letters follow a c, the order is e-i.

questions.question: What is the plural of "child"?
questions.explanation: "Child" has the irregular plural form "children."

questions.question: What does the idiom "break the ice" mean?
questions.explanation: "Break the ice" means to say or do something to relieve tension and begin social interaction or conversation.

questions.question: Who wrote the play "Romeo and Juliet"?
questions.explanation: William Shakespeare wrote the tragedy "Romeo and Juliet" in the 1590s.

questions.question: Which of these is a proper noun?
questions.explanation: "London" names one specific place, so it is a proper noun and is capitalized; the others are common nouns.

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: "She ___ to school every day."
questions.explanation: With the third-person singular subject "she," the present-tense verb takes an -s, giving "goes."

questions.question: What is the antonym of "generous"?
questions.explanation: "Stingy" means unwilling to give or share, the opposite of "generous."

questions.question: What part of speech is the word "beautiful"?
questions.explanation: "Beautiful" describes a noun (for example, a beautiful garden), so it is an adjective.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
questions.explanation: "It's" is the contraction of "it is," so "It's a sunny day" is correct. "Its" without an apostrophe is the possessive form.

questions.question: Which word is a synonym for "diligent"?
questions.explanation: "Diligent" means showing careful and persistent effort, which matches "hardworking."

questions.question: What does the idiom "let the cat out of the bag" mean?
questions.explanation: "Let the cat out of the bag" means to accidentally disclose a secret.

questions.question: Who wrote the novel "Pride and Prejudice"?
questions.explanation: Jane Austen wrote "Pride and Prejudice," published in 1813.

questions.question: Which of the following is a complete sentence?
questions.explanation: "The dog barked loudly" has a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought; the others are sentence fragments.

questions.question: What is the past tense of "go"?
questions.explanation: "Go" is an irregular verb whose simple past tense is "went" ("gone" is the past participle).

questions.question: Which word is an example of an oxymoron?
questions.explanation: "Bittersweet" combines two contradictory ideas (bitter and sweet), making it an oxymoron.

questions.question: What figure of speech makes a comparison using "like" or "as"?
questions.explanation: A simile compares two things using the words "like" or "as," as in "brave as a lion." A metaphor compares without those words.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: "___ going to the park later."
questions.explanation: "They're" is the contraction of "they are," which fits the sentence's meaning.

questions.question: Which is the correct spelling?
questions.explanation: "Conscientious," meaning careful and thorough, is spelled c-o-n-s-c-i-e-n-t-i-o-u-s.

questions.question: Who wrote the dystopian novel "1984"?
questions.explanation: George Orwell wrote "1984," published in 1949. Huxley wrote "Brave New World" and Bradbury wrote "Fahrenheit 451."

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a semicolon?
options: To join two related independent clauses
questions.explanation: A semicolon links two closely related independent clauses that could each stand alone as a sentence. Introducing a list is typically the job of a colon.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: "If I ___ you, I would apologize."
questions.explanation: The subjunctive mood uses "were" for hypothetical or contrary-to-fact situations, even with a singular subject like "I."

questions.question: In the phrase "a run of bad luck," what part of speech is "run"?
questions.explanation: Here "run" names a continuous period or spell and is preceded by the article "a," so it functions as a noun.

questions.question: Neither the manager nor the employees ___ satisfied with the decision.
questions.explanation: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, here the plural "employees," so "are" is correct.

questions.question: Each of the students ___ a laptop for the course.
questions.explanation: "Each" is grammatically singular, so it requires the singular verb "has," regardless of the plural "students" in the of-phrase.

questions.question: The number of applicants ___ increased sharply this year.
questions.explanation: "The number of" is a singular subject (the figure itself) and takes the singular verb "has."

questions.question: A number of students ___ absent from class today.
questions.explanation: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb, "are."

questions.question: Mathematics ___ my favorite subject in school.
questions.explanation: Academic subjects ending in "-ics" are treated as singular, so "is" is correct.

questions.question: Neither of the answers ___ correct, according to the key.
questions.explanation: "Neither" is grammatically singular, so formal usage requires the singular verb "is."

questions.question: Ten miles ___ a long way to walk in one day.
questions.explanation: A distance treated as a single measured unit takes a singular verb, so "is" is correct.

questions.question: The scissors ___ on the kitchen table.
questions.explanation: "Scissors" is a plural-only (bipartite) noun and requires "are."

questions.question: The jury ___ reached its verdict after two days.
questions.explanation: The pronoun "its" signals the collective noun is treated as a single unit, requiring the singular "has."

questions.question: There ___ a number of reasons for the delay.
questions.explanation: In existential "there" sentences the verb agrees with the postposed subject, here the plural "reasons," so "are" is correct.

questions.question: Bread and butter ___ a common breakfast in that region.
questions.explanation: "Bread and butter" names a single combined dish, so it takes a singular verb.

questions.question: More than one house ___ been sold on this street.
questions.explanation: Despite its plural sense, the fixed phrase "more than one + singular noun" idiomatically takes a singular verb.

questions.question: Between you and ___, the plan is deeply flawed.
questions.explanation: As the object of the preposition "between," the objective pronoun "me" is required.

questions.question: ___ do you think will win the election?
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of "will win" ("I think ___ will win"); "do you think" is a parenthetical insertion, so the subjective "Who" is correct.

questions.question: The award went to ___ scored the highest.
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of "scored" within the noun clause; the whole clause, not the pronoun, is the object of "to," so "whoever" is correct.

questions.question: She is considerably taller than ___.
questions.explanation: In formal usage the comparison is elliptical for "than he is," so the subjective "he" is preferred.

questions.question: It was ___ who first raised the objection.
questions.explanation: As a predicate nominative after the linking verb "was," formal usage takes the subjective "I."

questions.question: ___ students deserve better funding from the college.
questions.explanation: The pronoun stands in apposition to the subject "students," so it takes the subjective "We."

questions.question: The teacher praised ___ for finishing early.
questions.explanation: Both pronouns are direct objects of "praised," so both must be objective: "him and me."

questions.question: ___ book did you borrow from the library?
questions.explanation: "Whose" is the possessive determiner asking which person's book; "who's" means "who is."

questions.question: The man ___ I met yesterday is a surgeon.
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun is the object of "met," so formal usage calls for the objective "whom."

questions.question: By the time we arrive, the show ___.
questions.explanation: The future perfect "will have started" describes an action completed before a future reference point.

questions.question: I ___ in this city for five years and still love it.
questions.explanation: The present perfect expresses a state that began in the past and continues up to now.

questions.question: When I got to the station, the train ___.
questions.explanation: The past perfect shows the departure occurred before the past moment of arriving.

questions.question: Look at those dark clouds! It ___.
questions.explanation: "Be going to" expresses a prediction based on present evidence.

questions.question: This time next week, I ___ on a beach in Spain.
questions.explanation: The future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time; "lie/lying" (recline) is the correct verb.

questions.question: She ___ tennis since she was six years old.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous stresses an activity continuing from a past starting point up to now.

questions.question: I wish I ___ more time to prepare yesterday.
questions.explanation: A wish regretting the past uses the past perfect "had had."

questions.question: He said he ___ the report by Friday.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, "will" backshifts to "would" as future-in-the-past.

questions.question: No sooner ___ the door than the phone rang.
questions.explanation: "No sooner" in front position forces subject-auxiliary inversion, and the correlative "than" pairs with the past perfect.

questions.question: By 2020, they ___ in that house for a decade.
questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous expresses a duration continuing up to a point in the past.

questions.question: I ___ to Paris three times, and I adore that city.
questions.explanation: "Have been" indicates completed visits with return, unlike "have gone," which implies still being away.

questions.question: While I ___ dinner, the doorbell rang.
questions.explanation: The past continuous sets an ongoing background action that a simple-past event interrupts.

questions.question: If I ___ you, I would apologize immediately.
questions.explanation: The second conditional uses the subjunctive "were" for a hypothetical present situation.

questions.question: If she ___ harder, she would have passed the exam.
questions.explanation: The third conditional uses "had + past participle" for an unreal past condition.

questions.question: ___ she called earlier, we could have helped her.
questions.explanation: Inverting the third conditional drops "if" and fronts the auxiliary "Had."

questions.question: If it ___ tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
questions.explanation: The first conditional uses the simple present in the if-clause even for future meaning.

questions.question: ___ you need anything, please call the front desk.
questions.explanation: Inverting a first-conditional if-clause uses "Should" to mean "if you should (happen to)."

questions.question: If I had accepted that job, I ___ rich now.
questions.explanation: This mixed conditional pairs a past condition with a present result, requiring "would be."

questions.question: ___ it not for your support, I would give up entirely.
questions.explanation: "Were it not for" is a fixed subjunctive inversion expressing a present unreal condition.

questions.question: I suggest that she ___ the offer without delay.
questions.explanation: The mandative subjunctive uses the base form "accept" after "suggest that," with no third-person -s.

questions.question: It is essential that every child ___ vaccinated.
questions.explanation: Adjectives of importance like "essential" trigger the base-form subjunctive "be."

questions.question: He behaves as though he ___ the owner of the company.
questions.explanation: "As though" describing a contrary-to-fact situation takes the subjunctive "were."

questions.question: Long ___ the queen!
questions.explanation: This fixed optative expression uses the base-form subjunctive "live" to express a wish.

questions.question: I wish it ___ not so, but the news is true.
questions.explanation: After "wish" about a present situation, the subjunctive "were" is used.

questions.question: She plays ___ violin beautifully in the orchestra.
questions.explanation: Names of musical instruments take the definite article "the" in the "play the (instrument)" construction.

questions.question: He was elected ___ president of the student council.
questions.explanation: A unique office or title following verbs like "elect" and "appoint" takes no article.

questions.question: I need ___ information about the course before enrolling.
questions.explanation: "Information" is uncountable, so "some" is correct; "a/an" and "few" require countable nouns.

questions.question: ___ Everest is the highest mountain on Earth.
questions.explanation: Individual mountain names take no article (contrast with ranges like "the Alps").

questions.question: He is ___ honest man, respected by everyone.
questions.explanation: Article choice follows the initial sound, not spelling; "honest" begins with a vowel sound (silent h), so "an" is used.

questions.question: ___ rich should do more to help the poor.
questions.explanation: "The" plus an adjective denotes a whole class of people ("the rich" = rich people).

questions.question: I bought ___ umbrella and ___ raincoat.
questions.explanation: "Umbrella" begins with a vowel sound (an) and "raincoat" with a consonant sound (a).

questions.question: She has ___ money left, so she can't afford the trip.
questions.explanation: "Little" (without "a") stresses an insufficient amount of an uncountable noun; "money" is uncountable, ruling out "few/a few."

questions.question: I have ___ close friends, so I'm rarely lonely.
questions.explanation: "A few" expresses a positive, sufficient number of a countable noun; "few" would imply almost none.

questions.question: Young children go to ___ school to learn to read.
questions.explanation: When referring to its primary institutional purpose rather than a specific building, "school" takes no article.

questions.question: I look forward to ___ from you soon.
questions.explanation: In "look forward to," "to" is a preposition and is followed by a gerund.

questions.question: She skillfully avoided ___ the difficult question.
questions.explanation: The verb "avoid" is always followed by a gerund.

questions.question: He decided ___ the meeting until Monday.
questions.explanation: The verb "decide" is followed by a to-infinitive.

questions.question: I distinctly remember ___ the door before we left.
questions.explanation: "Remember" plus a gerund refers to recalling an action already done.

questions.question: Please remember ___ the letter on your way to work.
questions.explanation: "Remember" plus a to-infinitive refers to a future task one must not forget.

questions.question: On the long drive, we stopped ___ some coffee.
questions.explanation: "Stop" plus a to-infinitive expresses the purpose of stopping (stop in order to get coffee).

questions.question: It's no use ___ over spilled milk.
questions.explanation: The expression "it's no use" is followed by a gerund.

questions.question: Her parents let her ___ the car on weekends.
questions.explanation: "Let" is followed by a bare (to-less) infinitive.

questions.question: I'd rather ___ at home tonight than go out.
questions.explanation: "Would rather" is followed by a bare infinitive.

questions.question: The overwhelming evidence made him ___ his mistake.
questions.explanation: In the active voice, "make (someone do)" is followed by a bare infinitive.

questions.question: I'm used to ___ up early for work.
questions.explanation: In "be used to," "to" is a preposition, so a gerund follows (contrast with "used to get," a past habit).

questions.question: The students were made ___ their homework again.
questions.explanation: In the passive voice, "be made" is followed by a to-infinitive, unlike its active bare-infinitive form.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
options: Walking into the room, the smell of fresh paint was overpowering.
Walking into the room, I noticed the smell of fresh paint.
When I walked into the room, the smell of fresh paint was overpowering.
The smell of fresh paint was overpowering as I walked into the room.
questions.explanation: In the first option the introductory phrase illogically modifies "the smell," which cannot walk; the others supply or imply a valid subject.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly repairs "Having finished the assignment, the TV was turned on"?
options: Having finished the assignment, I turned on the TV.
Having finished the assignment, the TV was turned on by me.
The TV was turned on, having finished the assignment.
Having finished the assignment, turning on the TV.
questions.explanation: Only the first option makes the grammatical subject ("I") the one who finished the assignment; option 2 still leaves "the TV" as the subject of the participle.

questions.question: Which sentence uses parallel structure correctly?
options: She enjoys hiking, swimming, and biking.
She enjoys hiking, swimming, and to bike.
She enjoys to hike, swimming, and biking.
She enjoys hike, swim, and biking.
questions.explanation: All three items are gerunds, keeping the list grammatically parallel.

questions.question: Which sentence contains faulty parallelism?
options: He is intelligent, witty, and works very hard.
He is intelligent, witty, and hardworking.
The task requires patience, skill, and dedication.
She spoke clearly, confidently, and persuasively.
questions.explanation: The first option mixes two adjectives with a finite verb phrase, breaking the parallel structure.

questions.question: The manager was responsible for hiring staff, training them, and ___ their performance.
questions.explanation: The gerund "evaluating" matches "hiring" and "training" to maintain parallelism.

questions.question: If you mean that she drove them on nearly every day, which sentence is correct?
options: She drove her kids to school almost every day.
She almost drove her kids to school every day.
She drove her kids almost to school every day.
Almost she drove her kids to school every day.
questions.explanation: Placing "almost" directly before "every day" correctly conveys "on nearly every day"; the other placements change the meaning or are ungrammatical.

questions.question: ___ the exam, but she also earned a scholarship.
questions.explanation: A clause beginning with the negative adverbial "not only" requires subject-auxiliary inversion ("did she pass").

questions.question: The proposal is both cost-effective and ___.
questions.explanation: "Both...and" requires parallel elements; since "cost-effective" is an adjective, another adjective ("time-saving") must follow.

questions.question: What does the adjective "ephemeral" most precisely mean?
options: Lasting for a very short time
questions.explanation: "Ephemeral" derives from Greek roots meaning "lasting only a day" and describes something transient or short-lived.

questions.question: A person described as "perfidious" is best characterized as:
questions.explanation: "Perfidious" means deliberately faithless, betraying trust, from Latin "perfidia" (breach of faith).

questions.question: If someone has a "sanguine" outlook, they are:
questions.explanation: "Sanguine" describes a hopeful, optimistic disposition, from the old belief that blood (Latin "sanguis") produced a cheerful temperament.

questions.question: A "laconic" reply is one that is:
questions.explanation: "Laconic" means using minimal words, from the terse speech reputed of the Laconians (Spartans).

questions.question: Someone behaving in an "obsequious" manner is being:
questions.explanation: "Obsequious" describes servile, sycophantic eagerness to please, from Latin "obsequi" (to comply).

questions.question: A "truculent" attitude is one that is:
options: Aggressively defiant and eager to fight
questions.explanation: "Truculent" means fierce, belligerent, and quick to argue or fight, from Latin "truculentus."

questions.question: Something "ineffable" is:
options: Too great or intense to be expressed in words
questions.explanation: "Ineffable" combines the prefix "in-" (not) with a Latin root meaning "speak" (fari), describing what defies verbal expression.

questions.question: A "pusillanimous" leader is best described as:
questions.explanation: "Pusillanimous" comes from Latin "pusillus" (very small) + "animus" (spirit), meaning faint-hearted or timid.

questions.question: A "mendacious" statement is one that is:
questions.explanation: "Mendacious" means given to lying or false, from Latin "mendax" (lying).

questions.question: A "fastidious" person is:
options: Very attentive to detail and hard to please
questions.explanation: "Fastidious" describes someone meticulous and demanding about accuracy and cleanliness.

questions.question: A "recalcitrant" employee is one who is:
options: Stubbornly resistant to authority or control
questions.explanation: "Recalcitrant" means obstinately defiant of authority, from Latin "recalcitrare" (to kick back).

questions.question: To call someone "perspicacious" is to say they are:
options: Having keen mental insight and discernment
questions.explanation: "Perspicacious" describes sharp perceptiveness and understanding, distinct from "perspicuous" (clearly expressed).

questions.question: A "munificent" gift is one that is:
questions.explanation: "Munificent" means characterized by great generosity, from Latin "munus" (gift) + "facere" (to make).

questions.question: An "insidious" threat is one that:
options: Proceeds gradually and harmfully in a concealed way
questions.explanation: "Insidious" describes harm that develops subtly and treacherously before its damage is noticed.

questions.question: A "nascent" industry is one that is:
questions.explanation: "Nascent" means coming into existence or in an early stage, from Latin "nasci" (to be born).

questions.question: "Diaphanous" fabric is best described as:
questions.explanation: "Diaphanous" means so fine as to be see-through, from Greek roots meaning "showing through."

questions.question: A "quotidian" concern is one that is:
questions.explanation: "Quotidian" means daily or ordinary, from Latin "quotidie" (every day).

questions.question: To "enervate" a person is to:
options: Drain them of strength and vitality
questions.explanation: Despite sounding like "energize," "enervate" means to weaken or exhaust, from Latin "enervare" (to remove the sinews).

questions.question: A "noisome" odor is one that is:
questions.explanation: "Noisome" derives from Middle English "noy" (a shortening of "annoy"), not "noise," and means harmful, disgusting, or foul-smelling.

questions.question: A "disinterested" judge is one who is:
options: Impartial and free from personal bias
questions.explanation: In careful usage, "disinterested" means unbiased or impartial, whereas "uninterested" means not caring.

questions.question: Someone who is "bemused" is:
questions.explanation: "Bemused" means confused or bewildered, not "amused," despite the similar sound.

questions.question: In traditional usage, to "peruse" a document means to:
options: Read or examine it carefully and thoroughly
questions.explanation: Traditionally "peruse" means to read with great care, the opposite of skimming.

questions.question: To be "nonplussed" is to be:
options: So surprised or confused that one is unsure how to react
questions.explanation: "Nonplussed" (from Latin "non plus," "no more") describes being so bewildered one cannot proceed.

questions.question: In traditional prescriptive usage, "enormity" refers to:
options: Extreme wickedness or the gravity of an offense
questions.explanation: Traditionally "enormity" denotes great moral wrongdoing rather than mere hugeness, for which "enormousness" is preferred.

questions.question: Something described as "ubiquitous" is:
questions.explanation: "Ubiquitous" means found everywhere, from Latin "ubique" (everywhere).

questions.question: Which word correctly completes the sentence: "The new regulation will ___ every employee in the company"?
questions.explanation: As a verb meaning "to influence," the correct word is "affect"; "effect" as a verb means "to bring about."

questions.question: Which sentence uses "fewer" and "less" correctly?
options: There were less cars but fewer traffic overall
There were fewer cars and less traffic overall
There were fewer cars but fewer traffic overall
There were less cars and less traffic overall
questions.explanation: "Fewer" modifies countable nouns (cars) and "less" modifies uncountable nouns (traffic).

questions.question: Which sentence uses "comprise" in the traditionally correct way?
options: The team is comprised of ten players
Ten players are comprised in the team
The team comprises of ten players
questions.explanation: Traditionally the whole "comprises" its parts; "is comprised of" is widely considered incorrect.

questions.question: Which word means "individually separate and distinct"?
questions.explanation: "Discrete" means separate or distinct, while "discreet" means careful and tactful.

questions.question: To openly and contemptuously disregard a rule is to ___ it.
questions.explanation: "Flout" means to openly disregard a rule, whereas "flaunt" means to display ostentatiously.

questions.question: In precise usage, a speaker ___ something and a listener ___ it.
questions.explanation: To "imply" is to suggest something indirectly; to "infer" is to draw a conclusion from evidence.

questions.question: Which word means "a fundamental truth or general law"?
questions.explanation: "Principle" is a noun meaning a basic truth or rule; "principal" means chief or a head of a school.

questions.question: Which word means "to draw out or evoke a response"?
questions.explanation: "Elicit" is a verb meaning to bring forth; "illicit" is an adjective meaning illegal or forbidden.

questions.question: Which word means "something that completes or perfectly pairs with another"?
questions.explanation: "Complement" means to complete, while "compliment" means an expression of praise.

questions.question: Which word refers to writing materials such as paper and envelopes?
questions.explanation: "Stationery" (with an 'e') means writing paper; "stationary" (with an 'a') means not moving.

questions.question: Which word means "strongly opposed to or disinclined toward something"?
questions.explanation: "Averse" describes a person's dislike or reluctance, while "adverse" describes unfavorable conditions.

questions.question: In careful usage, which verb means "to make certain that something happens"?
questions.explanation: "Ensure" means to guarantee an outcome; "insure" relates to insurance, and "assure" means to tell someone confidently.

questions.question: In traditional usage, which word refers to physical distance?
questions.explanation: "Farther" traditionally refers to literal, measurable distance, while "further" refers to figurative or additional degree.

questions.question: Which verb correctly completes: "I need to ___ down for a rest" (to recline oneself)?
questions.explanation: "Lie" is intransitive (to recline) and takes no object, whereas "lay" is transitive and requires a direct object.

questions.question: Which word means "to make something bad less severe"?
questions.explanation: "Mitigate" means to lessen severity; "militate" means to be a strong influencing factor (usually against something).

questions.question: Which word is the closest synonym for "garrulous"?
questions.explanation: Both "garrulous" and "loquacious" mean excessively talkative.

questions.question: Which word is the closest synonym for "obdurate"?
questions.explanation: "Obdurate" and "intransigent" both mean stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion.

questions.question: Which word is the closest synonym for "abstruse"?
questions.explanation: "Abstruse" and "recondite" both describe something difficult to understand or obscure.

questions.question: Which word is the closest synonym for "ameliorate"?
questions.explanation: "Ameliorate" means to make a bad situation better, i.e., to improve.

questions.question: Which word is the closest synonym for "parsimonious"?
questions.explanation: "Parsimonious" means excessively frugal or stingy, a close synonym of "miserly."

questions.question: Which word is the closest synonym for "capricious"?
questions.explanation: "Capricious" and "mercurial" both describe someone given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior.

questions.question: Which word is the closest synonym for "surfeit"?
questions.explanation: A "surfeit" is an excessive amount or overindulgence.

questions.question: Which word is the closest synonym for "pellucid"?
questions.explanation: Both "pellucid" and "limpid" mean transparently clear.

questions.question: Which word is the best antonym of "profligate"?
questions.explanation: "Profligate" means recklessly wasteful, so its antonym is "frugal" (economical).

questions.question: Which word is the best antonym of "gregarious"?
questions.explanation: "Gregarious" means fond of company, so "reclusive" (preferring solitude) is its antonym.

questions.question: Which word is the best antonym of "verbose"?
questions.explanation: "Verbose" means using too many words, so its antonym is "concise."

questions.question: Which word is the best antonym of "exacerbate"?
questions.explanation: "Exacerbate" means to make worse, so "alleviate" (to ease) is its antonym.

questions.question: Which word is the best antonym of "laud"?
questions.explanation: "Laud" means to praise highly, so "censure" (to criticize severely) is its antonym.

questions.question: Which word is the best antonym of "nadir"?
questions.explanation: "Nadir" is the lowest point, while "zenith" is the highest point.

questions.question: When the moon is said to "wax," its opposite process is to:
questions.explanation: To "wax" means to grow larger; its antonym "wane" means to grow smaller or diminish.

questions.question: Which word is the best antonym of "candid"?
questions.explanation: "Candid" means openly honest, so "evasive" (avoiding directness) is its antonym.
